r1: On the Moon and on Mars, there are machines NASA left behind. A lander from 1967. Rovers parked by astronauts. A little helicopter that flew 72 times. They're abandoned, but not forgotten: each one still tells us what those worlds do to the things we build.
r2: When Apollo 12 landed next to Surveyor 3, the crew brought pieces of it home. After 31 months on the Moon, they were darkened by dust and sunlight, but nothing had seriously failed. Later, Apollo 17's rover lost a fender, and the astronauts fixed it with maps and tape. Up there, there are no spare parts.
s1: On the Moon, a broken wrench is not a small problem. The next one is 384,000 kilometres away, and sending it can cost up to a million dollars per kilogram.
s2: In 2026, NASA Glenn grew a plastic inside bacteria and mixed it with simulated Moon and Mars dust: a material that could be made on site. But which mix? How much dust, and is it strong enough for a wrench? You can't test every combination on Earth.
s3: So, for the Abandoned but not Forgotten challenge, we built the Moon-Material Simulator. Pick a binder, a soil, and how the part is made. Instantly, a physics model corrected by machine learning predicts eight properties, shows how sure it is, and tells you whether each number is backed by real lab data. It runs in any browser, and it's open source.
s4: Our science stands on NASA's own data: NASA Glenn's bacterial-plastic reports, NASA Kennedy's regolith-printing studies, a 2003 NASA report, and peer-reviewed papers. We transcribed 1,470 measured values, each tied to its page. Then we built an auditor that finds every number again in the original PDF. It never edits data. Zero transcription errors, and 181 problems inside the papers themselves.
s5: Physics alone isn't enough: on real samples, its compressive-strength error averaged 230 percent. So we kept the physics and taught a Gaussian process its mistakes, using 152 real measurements. On mixes it never saw, that error drops from 230 to 34 percent, stiffness from 65 to 19, and density from 16 to 5. A completely new study is harder, and we say so. And every prediction links to its evidence: we predict 117 megapascals, and the paper measured 119.
s6a: Back to our wrench: NASA's bioplastic with 38 percent lunar dust. It breaks at 71 newtons, just short of the 72 needed to tighten a bolt. At lunar noon it softens to a sixth of that. At lunar night it's almost twice as strong, but brittle: it snaps instead of bending.
s6b: So we ask the optimizer. It tests nearly five thousand mixes and finds one made entirely from local resources: 45 percent dust and 15 percent basalt fibre. Safety factor 1.7, and it bends before it breaks.
s6c: Ask it for a rocket nozzle, and it honestly says no plastic survives. But a kit of 25 small parts printed on site keeps 10 kilograms off the launch pad: up to 10 million dollars.
team: We're Dreams of X. Mahdin Islam Mukim, team lead. Maliha Sanjana, design. Lamisa Yeasmin Nakia, research and storytelling. And the two who built most of it: Yousuf Abdullah, AI and data science, and Habibullah Sharif, the simulator itself.
s7: The machines we left behind taught us what the Moon does to materials. Now our simulator helps engineers choose the right mix before a single sample is printed, and shows the real measurement behind every answer. The same method works for Mars. Try it yourself.
